seo.best_title: Where Did Ancient Humans Go to the Toilet?
seo.description_hook: Where did ancient humans go to the toilet before plumbing, toilet paper and locks on the door? The answer involves a toilet demon, a sponge on a stick, and a tax on pee.
paragraphs: In this animated history explainer we follow the toilet from the Stone Age to the first flush: what early humans did in the wild, the first toilets of Mesopotamia, the surprisingly modern plumbing of the Indus Valley, and Rome's famous group latrines.

Then we go to ancient China, where archaeologists found a 2,400-year-old flush toilet in a palace, and to medieval Europe, where chamber pots, castle toilets and the 'gong farmers' who cleaned them made life very smelly.
Ancient hygiene, ancient sanitation, the history of toilet paper and everyday life in the past, explained simply with stick figures and a bit of dry humour.
sources: Augusta McMahon - Trash and Toilets in Mesopotamia, The Ancient Near East Today (2016)
Ann Olga Koloski-Ostrow - The Archaeology of Sanitation in Roman Italy (2015)
Charlier et al. - Toilet hygiene in the classical era, BMJ (2012)
Sistiaga et al. - The Neanderthal Meal: A New Perspective Using Faecal Biomarkers, PLOS ONE (2014)
Jonathan Mark Kenoyer - Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
Yueyang palace flush toilet find, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, reported by Live Science (2023)

shots.say: Right now, a toilet is the most boring room in your house.
It flushes. It has paper. It even has a lock.
But ten thousand years ago? None of that existed.
No pipes. No paper. No privacy.
shots.ai: a worried stick figure standing alone in a jungle, thinking about a toilet

shots.say: So where did ancient humans actually go?
Today we follow the toilet through history.

shots.title: COMING UP
shots.say: There's a toilet demon, a sponge on a stick, and a tax on pee.
Yes, really. Let's go.
For most of human history, the answer was simple.
You walked away from camp. That's it. That was the bathroom.
shots.ai: a stick figure in fur clothes walking away from a stone age camp toward some bushes

shots.say: And there was one important rule. Distance.
Groups of hunter-gatherers moved around a lot.
When a camp got too dirty, they just left.

shots.label: COPROLITE
shots.say: And here's the weird part. We know some of this from fossil poop.
Yes. Scientists study fossil poop. It's called a coprolite.

shots.label: EL SALT
shots.say: At a site in Spain called El Salt...
...researchers found Neanderthal poop about fifty thousand years old.

shots.title: NEANDERTHAL MENU
shots.say: It showed they ate mostly meat, but also plants.
Somebody had to check that. That person is a hero.
Which brings us to the question you're already asking.
What did they wipe with?

shots.title: STONE AGE OPTIONS
shots.say: Leaves. Moss. Grass. Smooth stones.
In cold places, snow.
shots.ai: a shocked stick figure in fur clothes in a snowy landscape

shots.say: Imagine living in the Ice Age and that's your only option.
Near the sea, people used shells.
shots.ai: a happy stick figure on a beach pointing at a big sea shell

shots.say: And in many cultures, the answer was simply water.
The key skill was knowing which leaves not to touch.
Then something changed. People started living in cities.
Thousands of people. In one place. Every single day.
You can see the problem.

shots.label: MESOPOTAMIA
shots.say: In Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq...
...some houses had toilets by about three thousand B C.

shots.title: MESOPOTAMIAN TOILET
shots.say: A seat over a pit, lined with clay rings to drain the waste.
Not bad. Honestly, not bad at all.
But in many neighborhoods, fewer than half the houses had one.

shots.label: SHULAK
shots.say: And the Babylonians had one more worry. A toilet demon.
His name was Shulak, and he lived in the bathroom.
If you got sick after using the toilet, Shulak got the blame.
To be fair, something invisible really was attacking them. It was germs.
But the real plumbing champions lived further east.

shots.label: MOHENJO-DARO
shots.say: In the Indus Valley, in today's Pakistan and India.
About four and a half thousand years ago...
...cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were planned on a grid.

shots.title: INDUS DRAINS
shots.say: Many homes had a toilet connected to covered drains in the street.
Covered drains. In the Bronze Age.
Some European cities wouldn't match that for thousands of years.
Now let's talk about the Romans. They made toilets social.
Public toilets had long stone benches with holes. No walls.
You sat next to strangers. And you chatted.
Business, gossip, dinner plans. All on the toilet.
shots.ai: two stick figures in togas chatting while sitting on a long stone bench toilet in ancient Rome

shots.title: UNDER THE BENCH
shots.say: Under the bench, water ran into the sewer.
And then there's the famous sponge on a stick.

shots.label: TERSORIUM
shots.say: It's called a tersorium. Roman writers mention it.
The popular story is that everyone shared the same sponge.
But here's the twist.
Some historians think it was actually a toilet brush.
For cleaning the toilet. Not the person. We're honestly not sure.

shots.title: ALSO USED
shots.say: We do know some Greeks and Romans wiped with pottery pebbles.
A study in a medical journal suggested these could cause injuries.
Which nobody needed a study to guess.
Rome also had another bathroom secret. Pee was valuable.
Pots were left in the street to collect urine.
shots.ai: a stick figure carrying a big clay pot through a Roman street

shots.title: WHY URINE?
shots.say: Laundry workers used it. The ammonia helped clean wool and cloth.
Yes. Your toga was washed in pee.
So Emperor Vespasian did what governments do. He taxed it.
A tax on pee.
When his son complained, the story says he held up a coin.
And said: money doesn't smell.

shots.label: XI'AN
shots.say: Meanwhile, in China, archaeologists found something amazing.
A flush toilet about two thousand four hundred years old.

shots.label: PALACE TOILET
shots.say: It was in a palace near Xi'an, with a pipe to a pit outside.
But it didn't flush itself. So who flushed it?
Servants. They poured water in after each use.
shots.ai: a bored stick figure servant carrying a water jar toward a palace toilet

shots.say: Worst job in the palace. Or is it?

shots.label: PIG TOILET
shots.say: Because in Han dynasty China, some toilets sat right above a pig pen.
shots.ai: an ancient Chinese house with a toilet room built directly above a pig pen with a pig

shots.say: You can guess what the pig ate.

shots.title: THE PIG LOOP
shots.say: Then people ate the pig. Recycling, but make it disgusting.
China also gave us the first written mention of toilet paper.

shots.title: TOILET PAPER
shots.say: A scholar mentioned it in the five hundreds. By thirteen ninety-three, the emperor's family had special paper.
Now, medieval Europe. Things got a little messy.
Most people used a chamber pot. A bucket for the bedroom.
And in some crowded towns, it was emptied out of the window.
shots.ai: a shocked stick figure on a medieval street as someone empties a chamber pot from a window above

shots.say: So when walking in town, you looked up.

shots.label: GARDEROBE
shots.say: Castles had toilets called garderobes, sticking out of the wall.
shots.ai: a medieval castle with a small toilet room sticking out from the wall high above a moat

shots.say: Everything dropped straight down into the moat.
Which made attacking the castle even less fun.
In England, someone had to clean the cesspits. They were called gong farmers.
shots.ai: two stick figures working at night cleaning a pit with buckets by torchlight

shots.say: They worked at night, and they were paid well. For obvious reasons.

scenes.chapter: The First Flush and What's Next

shots.say: Finally, in fifteen ninety-six...
...an Englishman, John Harington, built a flushing toilet for Queen Elizabeth the first.
It worked! And almost nobody copied it for two hundred years.
Classic.

shots.title: THE LONG ROAD
shots.say: From leaves, to clay pipes, to sponges, to the flush.
So the next time you're in that boring little room...
...remember. No demon. No sponge. No pig.
But wait. If they had no soap, how did ancient people stay clean?
That's the next video. You might not like the answer.
